tagline.text: A cold, clear tiered waterfall at the foot of Mt. Banahaw in Majayjay

duration.label: Time needed
duration.text: Half day to full day trip

budget.label: Budget
budget.text: About ₱800–1,500 (day trip from Manila by public transport; rough estimate)

children.text: Taytay Falls is a waterfall in Barangay Gagalot, Majayjay, Laguna, also called Majayjay Falls or Imelda Falls. The water coming down from Mt. Banahaw is very cold and clear, and about 10 minutes' walk from the entrance brings you to the first fall.

Taytay Falls is a waterfall in Barangay Gagalot in Majayjay, Laguna. Its official name is Majayjay Falls, but locals more often call it Taytay Falls, and it is also known as Imelda Falls. Wikipedia explains that this name comes from former First Lady Imelda Marcos having financed tourism promotion there. Majayjay lies in southeastern Laguna, about 107 km from Manila and about 62 km from Santa Cruz.

The falls sit in forest at the foot of Mt. Banahaw, and the water is very cold and clear. A mountaineering blog written in 2007 gave the height as about 12 m and described a series of seven falls, with a wide, clear pool at the seventh as you climb. Wikipedia, on the other hand, describes a two-tier waterfall in a forested area. Because sources describe it differently, what you actually see on site may differ. The 2007 account says the first fall is about
10 minutes
on foot from the entrance and the last about
30 minutes
. A 2025 guide describes a walk of about
10 minutes
on a paved path from the registration area, which seems to refer to the approach to the first fall.

In Majayjay town stands the Spanish-era Church of Saint Gregory the Great. According to Wikipedia, Pope Francis designated it a minor basilica on January 25, 2025. If you do not want to see only the falls, take a look at the church in town as well. Other attractions mentioned include Bukal Falls, Mt. Banahaw and the Botocan Hydroelectric Power Plant and Dam. Majayjay was a Tagalog town before the Spanish arrived, and according to Wikipedia, in 1571 Spanish forces attacked it with Cebuano Visayan reinforcements. Its population was about 28,504 in 2024, a small mountain town, and the area around the falls is relatively quiet as a result.

There are reports that it gets very crowded and noisy with local families on weekends and during Holy Week. For a quieter visit, a weekday early morning is recommended. The water is too cold to swim for long, but just soaking in the pool below the falls takes the heat off. Fees and opening hours change from year to year, so check the latest information. The water coming down from Mt. Banahaw is cold all year round. A 2007 account says the first pool is about 3 m (10 feet) deep yet so clear that you can see a coin on the bottom. Wade in slowly at first before you get in.

Going up beyond the first fall, the falls continue, and a 2007 account describes one section where you descend by holding a vine and another where you scramble up using the rocks. The upper sections are slippery, so follow the advice of the local attendants.

blocks.title: A short walk from the entrance

children.text: After paying at the Gagalot registration area, you walk to the falls on a paved path and steps. There are handrails, but reports say it is slippery in the rain, so hold children's hands.

There is a large campsite near the falls, and many people pitch tents and spend the night. A 2025 guide says the designated camping area has no electricity and takes roughly 20 tents a night. On weekends it can be noisy with group campers.

There are restrooms, showers and changing rooms (cold water), and cottages and picnic tables can be used. Small shops and food stalls open on weekends but are reportedly almost absent on weekdays, so bring your own food. Cottages are first-come, first-served, so arrive early on weekends to claim one. blocks.title: Saint Gregory the Great Church, Majayjay

children.text: Built in the Spanish colonial period, it is known as one of the oldest churches in the Philippines. Wikipedia says Laguna de Bay can be seen from the church roof. On the way to the falls, take a look at the exterior and the plaza in front.

Also in southeastern Laguna are the shoe town of Liliw and the Nagcarlan Underground Cemetery, and one guide says the cemetery is about 20 minutes by car from the falls. After a half day at the falls, adding these two in the afternoon makes an efficient plan.

items.title: Day trip by public transport
items.subtitle: Changing at Santa Cruz for Gagalot

children.text: Take a DLTB or Green Star bus to Sta. Cruz from Buendia (Taft corner) or EDSA in Manila. Without traffic it takes about
2.5–3 hours
In Santa Cruz, take a jeepney to Majayjay. One guide says you can transfer to a Majayjay-bound jeepney along the road.
In Majayjay town, change to a jeepney or tricycle to Gagalot. Ask for "Taytay Falls" locally to be understood.
At the Gagalot registration area, write your name in the logbook and pay the entrance fee. Then walk the paved path to the first fall.
Swim in the pool, have lunch, then look at the upper falls.
Head down before sunset and return to Manila. Check the last bus times locally.
Public transport involves many transfers, so a one-way trip can take more than 4 hours. If possible, use a private car or a van. Leaving central Manila around 5 a.m. is safest.

items.title: One-night camping
items.subtitle: Pitch a tent under the stars

children.text: Leave Manila by car and stock up on groceries in Majayjay town. There are not many shops near the falls.
Register for camping at the registration area and pitch your tent in the designated area.
Swim at the falls before sunset.
The next morning, when few people are around, look at the upper falls and head home.
The campsite has no electricity and weak mobile signal. Bring a headlamp and a power bank.
Take a bus to Sta. Cruz from the Buendia–Taft corner or from Cubao in Manila. A 2025 guide gives the fare as about
and the trip as
2.5–3 hours
In Santa Cruz transfer to a jeepney to Majayjay, and in Majayjay town take a jeepney or tricycle to Gagalot. A 2025 guide gives the tricycle from Majayjay town to Gagalot as
shared or
chartered.
A 2025 guide says you can get from Calamba to Santa Cruz by van or jeepney for about
. After that it is the same jeepney and tricycle legs.
The whole one-way trip can take 4–5 hours. There is waiting time at each transfer, so leave early.
Take NLEX, the Skyway and SLEX, exit at Calamba, then go through Los Baños, Pila and Santa Cruz to Majayjay. A 2013 guide gave the SLEX toll from Calamba as
(Class 1 vehicle), though it may have changed since.
From Santa Cruz head toward Pagsanjan, pass Magdalena, enter Majayjay town and follow the signs for Gagalot. The last 5–10 km are winding mountain road.
Parking, as of 2025, is reported at
for cars and
for motorcycles.
At the Gagalot registration area (near the barangay hall), sign the logbook and pay the entrance fee.
Then walk a few hundred meters on a paved path and steps to the falls. It is slippery in the rain.
November–April, the dry season, is said to have the safest paths and the clearest water. You can go from May to October, but the current is stronger and the paths are slippery.
The water is spring water from Mt. Banahaw and very cold all year round. Even in hot March–May it is cool, but Holy Week and weekends are crowded.

Small shops and stalls open on weekends but are almost absent on weekdays. Buy a packed lunch and water in Majayjay town beforehand. You can also find places to eat in nearby Liliw or Nagcarlan.
When asking directions, say "Taytay Falls" rather than "Majayjay Falls."
Bring small bills (₱20 and ₱50). Shops cannot make change for large notes.
Pack non-slip shoes, a waterproof bag, a warm layer and a headlamp.
The water is very cold, so children and older visitors should wade in slowly.
Mobile signal is weak, so download offline maps.
A weekday early morning is the quietest. Check lodging in advance for long weekends.
Do not forget the registration step of writing your name in the village logbook.
The basic rules are to sign the registration logbook, take your trash home and keep quiet hours. Follow the attendants' instructions first.
During or just after rain, the current gets stronger and the paths are very slippery. Avoid entering the water and follow the attendants' instructions.
Diving and cliff jumping are advised against because of hidden rocks and currents.
Soap and shampoo are banned in many streams, so follow the rules.
Guides say littering may be fined. Take your trash with you.

Two 2025–2026 guides say the site closes on Tuesday mornings (06:00–12:00) for maintenance. It may also close temporarily the day after heavy rain when the water is muddy and strong, so check locally before you visit.
Alcohol, smoking and campfires at the campsite may be restricted, so follow the rules.
The water is spring-fed and very cold, so get out often and dry off to avoid getting chilled.
A town famous for its shoe and slipper shops, close to the falls and good to add to an afternoon plan.
A Spanish-era underground cemetery that one guide says is about
20 minutes
by car from the falls. Check opening hours locally.
Laguna's best-known waterfall, famous for its gorge boat tour. Many people combine it into the same trip.
It has attractions such as the Church of Saint Gregory the Great and Bukal Falls.
